detail: The Targeted Anti-Avoidance Rule (TAAR), introduced in 2016, can reclassify MVL distributions as income (not capital gains) if the same trade is resumed through a new company within two years.
verified_quote: the individual receiving the distribution continues to carry on, or be involved with, the same trade or a trade similar to that of the wound-up company at any time within two years from the date of the distribution
notes: The Targeted Anti-Avoidance Rule (TAAR) was introduced by the Finance Act 2016 and applies to distributions made on or after April 6, 2016. It reclassifies distributions from a winding-up as income rather than capital gains if specific conditions are met. One of these conditions (Condition C) states that the individual receiving the distribution must not carry on or be involved with the same or a similar trade as the wound-up company within two years from the date of the distribution. This directly supports the claim that resuming the same trade through a new company within two years can lead to reclassification as income. The other conditions that must be met for TAAR to apply are: Condition A: The individual had at least a 5% interest in the company immediately before winding up. Condition B: The company was a close company at any point in the two years ending with the start of the winding up. Condition D: It is reasonable to assume that the main purpose, or one of the main purposes, of the winding-up is the avoidance or reduction of a charge to Income Tax.. The effective date of the TAAR legislation is April 6, 2016.. The primary authoritative source is HMRC internal manual which details the conditions for TAAR.

detail: The Declaration of Solvency must be made within five weeks before the winding-up resolution is passed.
verified_quote: A majority of the company's directors must make a statutory declaration of solvency in the 5 weeks before a resolution to wind up the company is passed.
notes: The GOV.UK guidance on Liquidation and insolvency, updated March 10, 2022, directly supports this claim. Section 6.1 states: "A majority of the company's directors must make a statutory declaration of solvency in the 5 weeks before a resolution to wind up the company is passed." This is also corroborated by The Insolvency Act 1986, Section 89(2)(a), which states the declaration must be made "within the 5 weeks immediately preceding the date of the passing of the resolution for winding up, or on that date but before the passing of the resolution".

detail: The winding-up resolution must be advertised in the London Gazette within 14 days of being passed.
verified_quote: When a company has passed a resolution for voluntary winding up, it shall, within 14 days after the passing of the resolution, give notice of the resolution by advertisement in the Gazette.
notes: This requirement is found in Section 85(1) of the Insolvency Act 1986, which is also reflected in GOV.UK guidance. The legislation is in force as of June 2026.

However, the specific notification to Companies House is governed by Section 109 of the Insolvency Act 1986 and typically uses forms like 600CH for England and Wales appointments after December 9, 2017.

detail: An overdrawn Director's Loan Account (DLA) is treated as a debt owed to the company, which the liquidator must pursue for creditors.
If an overdrawn DLA is not repaid within nine months of the company's year-end, the company may incur a Section 455 tax charge (currently 33.75%).
An overdrawn DLA exceeding £10,000 without interest can attract a benefit-in-kind tax for the director.
If a director continues to withdraw money from an overdrawn DLA when the company is insolvent, it could be treated as wrongful trading or misfeasance.

HMRC can issue Joint and Several Liability Notices (JSLNs) making directors personally liable for company tax debts in specific circumstances, including repeated insolvencies and tax liabilities exceeding £10,000.

HMRC can issue Personal Liability Notices (PLNs) under Section 121C of the Social Security Administration Act 1992, making directors personally liable for unpaid National Insurance Contributions if the underpayment was due to their fraud or neglect.
